content: The systematic review included studies from six databases: Embase, ERIC, PubMed, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science. Eligible studies were published in English, Spanish, or Portuguese between 2000 and 2016. The inclusion criteria required studies to involve children or adolescents aged 6–18 years, use school grades or standardized test scores as outcomes, and assess physical activity or cardiorespiratory fitness either through self-reports or objective measures. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and intervention studies were included, but studies with fewer than 30 participants were excluded. Two assessors independently reviewed titles and abstracts, followed by full-text articles. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Study quality was evaluated using the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies. A total of 51 articles were identified: 41 cross-sectional, 8 longitudinal, and 2 intervention studies. Half of the studies used school grades as the outcome variable, while the other half used standardized test scores. Eleven studies included objective assessments of physical activity and academic achievement, but the evidence was inconsistent. Eighteen studies used self-reported physical activity measures, with 12 reporting a positive association between physical activity and academic achievement. Twenty-eight studies examined the relationship between cardiorespiratory fitness and academic achievement, generally finding a positive association, though causation was unclear. The review noted limitations, including the narrative synthesis approach, lack of ranking studies by size, and potential bias in teacher-assessed grades, which are not standardized across schools. The findings supported a positive association between self-reported physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and academic achievement. However, objective measures of physical activity showed inconsistent associations. Importantly, physical activity did not negatively impact academic achievement. A systematic review by Martin and Murtagh (2017) examined the effects of integrating physical activity into school lessons on physical activity, academic, and health outcomes. The review included studies published between 1990 and 2015, focusing on classroom-based physical activity interventions that incorporated academic content. Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria, with six reporting medium-to-large effect sizes for physical activity levels. Four studies showed positive effects on learning outcomes, and three studies reported improved on-task behavior. Positive effects on students' BMI levels were also observed. Both students and teachers expressed satisfaction with the programs. The review concluded that physically active academic lessons increased physical activity levels and potentially benefited learning and health outcomes, emphasizing the need for such interventions in public health policy. A systematic review by Miguel-Berges et al. (2018) investigated the association between pedometer-determined physical activity and adiposity in children and adolescents. Of 304 eligible articles, 36 were included, with most being cross-sectional studies. The majority (72%) reported significant negative associations between walking and adiposity, supporting the hypothesis that higher levels of walking protect against obesity. However, prospective longitudinal studies are needed, particularly in younger children, to establish dose-response evidence. A systematic review by Mohammadi et al. (2019) explored the associations between diet, physical activity, and cardiometabolic risk factors in Malaysian adolescents. Seventeen studies were included, all of which were of poor quality. Physical activity was assessed in ten studies, primarily using self-reported questionnaires. Evidence linking physical activity to cardiometabolic health was weak, with some studies reporting associations with BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference. Sedentary behavior was assessed in two studies, with mixed findings. The review highlighted the need for higher-quality research in this area. A meta-analysis by Pozuelo-Carrascosa et al. (2018) synthesized evidence on the effectiveness of school-based physical activity interventions on cardiometabolic risk factors in children. Nineteen randomized controlled trials involving 11,988 children aged 3–12 years were included. The interventions improved some cardiometabolic risk factors, such as waist circumference, diastolic blood pressure, and fasting insulin levels. However, limitations included a lack of detailed descriptions of intervention implementation and compliance rates. The review emphasized the need for well-designed studies to optimize the effectiveness of school-based physical activity programs. A systematic review by Singh et al. (2019) examined the effects of physical activity interventions on cognitive and academic performance in children. Of 58 included studies, 11 were rated as high quality. Beneficial effects of physical activity on cognitive performance were observed in 48% of constructs analyzed, while 60% of analyses found significant positive effects on academic performance. Strong evidence supported the benefits of physical activity on mathematics performance. The review concluded that more high-quality research is needed to establish causality and guide future interventions. A systematic review by Skrede et al. (2019) summarized evidence on the prospective relationship between objectively measured sedentary time, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, and cardiometabolic risk factors in youth. The review emphasized the importance of understanding these relationships to inform interventions aimed at improving cardiometabolic health in children and adolescents.
